entries.title: GALOY
entries.body: Company founded in 2019 by Nicolas Burtey and Chris Hunter, developing open source Bitcoin banking infrastructure. Galoy is the origin of the Blink wallet (formerly “Bitcoin Beach Wallet”), the application that served as the foundation of the Bitcoin circular economy in El Zonte, El Salvador, before the country adopted bitcoin as legal tender in 2021. The Galoy platform allows organizations to deploy their own Bitcoin and Lightning banking infrastructure, either self-hosted or as a managed service (*Banking-as-a-Service*). The company also develops bitcoin-backed lending solutions.

entries.title: GAP LIMIT
entries.body:
Parameter used in Bitcoin wallet software to determine the maximum number of consecutive unused addresses to generate before ceasing to search for additional transactions. Adjusting this parameter is often necessary when recovering a wallet to ensure that all transactions are found. An insufficient Gap Limit could cause some transactions to be missed if addresses were skipped during the derivation phases. Increasing the Gap Limit allows the wallet to search further in the address sequence, in order to retrieve all associated transactions. 

Indeed, a single `xpub` can theoretically derive more than 4 billion receiving addresses (internal and external addresses). However, wallet software cannot derive all of them and check their usage without incurring an enormous operational cost. They therefore proceed in index order, because this is normally the order in which all wallet software generates addresses. The software records each used address before moving on to the next, and it stops its search when it encounters a number of consecutively empty addresses. This number is what is called the Gap Limit. 

If, for example, the Gap Limit is set to `20`, and address `m/84'/0'/0'/0/15/` is empty, the wallet will derive addresses up to `m/84'/0'/0'/0/34/`. If this range of addresses remains unused, the search stops there. Consequently, a transaction using address `m/84'/0'/0'/0/40/` would not be detected in this example.

entries.title: GATEWAY NODE
entries.body:
Lightning routing node that operates private (unannounced) channels to create additional routing opportunities. Unlike a classic routing node whose channels are all public and visible in the network graph, a *gateway node* also maintains private channels with other nodes. These channels are not broadcast via the *gossip* protocol, and therefore do not appear in the public topology of the network.

The value of a *gateway node* becomes apparent when other nodes open public channels to it: these connections create payment paths passing through the private channels, thus offering alternative routes invisible to the rest of the network. The *gateway node* then acts as a bridge between the public network and nodes that do not wish to expose their channels.

entries.title: GCS - GOLOMB-CODED SET
entries.body:
Probabilistic data structure used in BIP-0158 to build *compact block filters* on Bitcoin. A GCS makes it possible to test whether an element belongs to a set, with the guarantee of finding any element that is present, but with a false positive probability of `1/M`.

The construction of a GCS takes place in several steps: the raw elements are first hashed with SipHash into 64-bit integers uniformly distributed over the range `[0, N \times M)`. The resulting values are sorted, then the differences between consecutive values are encoded using Golomb-Rice coding. This coding exploits the natural geometric distribution of the gaps to achieve near-optimal compression: each difference is decomposed into a quotient (encoded in unary) and a remainder (encoded on `P` bits).

Compared to the Bloom filters used in BIP-0037, the GCS produces more compact filters for the same false positive rate. In exchange, the membership test requires sequentially decompressing the filter, which prevents constant-time queries. This structure was chosen for *compact block filters* with the parameters `P = 19` and `M = 784\,931`.

entries.title: GENESIS
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Genesis designates the set of initial data, governed by a specific schema, that establishes the starting state of any contract. This information constitutes the anchor point from which the evolution of smart contracts and the management of RGB tokens take place. It can be compared to the concept of the *Genesis Block* on Bitcoin, or to the concept of a Coinbase transaction, but here at the *client-side* level and for RGB tokens.

entries.title: GENESIS BLOCK
entries.body:
The Genesis block is the first block of the Bitcoin system. It embodies the concrete launch of Bitcoin. The Genesis block was created by Bitcoin's anonymous founder, Satoshi Nakamoto, on January 3, 2009. Its hash is:

```text
000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f
```

This block contains only one coinbase transaction, which generates 50 bitcoins as a reward for the miner (in this case, Satoshi Nakamoto himself). This block includes a message embedded in the coinbase transaction:

```text
The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks
```

This quote is a reference to an article in the newspaper *The Times*. The message is interpreted as a criticism of the traditional financial system and its excesses, which partly motivated the creation of Bitcoin as a monetary alternative.

Since it embodies the very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, the Genesis block has a field containing the hash of the previous block, but it is filled with zeros, because there is no previous block. Moreover, the 50 bitcoins generated as a reward in this block are not spendable at the protocol level.

entries.title: GETBLOCKTEMPLATE
entries.body:
Communication protocol between a Bitcoin node and mining software, defined in BIP-0022 and BIP-0023. It was introduced in 2012 to replace the `getwork` protocol, whose limitations were becoming problematic as the network's computing power grew.

Unlike `getwork`, which provided the miner with a block header ready to hash, `getblocktemplate` transmits a complete block model (*block template*). The miner receives the list of transactions to include, the block parameters and the consensus rules to follow. This approach allows the miner to build the candidate block themselves and to choose which transactions to include in it.

This change reduced the power of mining pool operators over transaction selection, which decentralized part of the block construction process. `getblocktemplate` was subsequently largely replaced by the Stratum protocol, then by Stratum V2.

entries.title: GETWORK
entries.body: Former mining protocol for Bitcoin created in 2010 by m0mchil. Getwork allowed miners to receive work data from a full node. It was built on RPC requests used to obtain block headers to work on in order to find a valid proof of work. Getwork was optimized for GPU mining. It was the first open source software designed to optimize communication between nodes and miners at a time when a few actors kept such software private. Getwork was gradually replaced by Stratum, which is more efficient, notably for ASICs, and less bandwidth-hungry.

entries.title: GHASH.IO
entries.body: Former Bitcoin mining pool operated by the company CEX.IO, based in the United Kingdom. Ghash.io is mainly known for having briefly exceeded 51% of the Bitcoin network's total hashrate in June 2014, raising concrete fears about the possibility of a 51% attack. Although the pool did not exploit this dominant position for malicious purposes, this event served as a wake-up call for the Bitcoin community, illustrating the centralization risks linked to mining pools. Many miners voluntarily left Ghash.io in the following days in order to redistribute the hashrate to other pools. Ghash.io then gradually lost importance before ceasing its activities.

entries.title: GINGER WALLET
entries.body: Ginger Wallet is an open source desktop Bitcoin wallet focused on privacy. It is a fork of Wasabi Wallet, launched in June 2024, a few days after zkSNACKs shut down its coinjoin coordination service. Ginger Wallet carries over Wasabi's privacy features, notably the integration of WabiSabi coinjoins.

entries.title: GIT
entries.body: Distributed version control system designed to efficiently manage any type of software project. It allows developers to track changes made to a project's source code over time, revert to earlier states, manage branches and merge changes. Git facilitates collaboration between developers by allowing several people to work on the same project simultaneously, with tools to manage any conflicts in files. Each developer works locally and can then synchronize their changes with the central repository. Created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, Git has become the de facto standard for version control in the software industry. The development of Bitcoin node implementations, including Bitcoin Core, is managed with Git.

entries.title: GITHUB
entries.body: Source code management and hosting platform that facilitates collaboration between developers. As its name indicates, GitHub is built on the Git version control system. This platform therefore makes it possible to track code changes, manage versions and encourage collaboration through tools such as pull requests and issues. GitHub has become an essential tool for developers, notably in the Bitcoin community where the majority of projects, including Bitcoin Core, the main implementation of the protocol, are hosted there. In 2018, Microsoft acquired GitHub for 7.5 billion dollars.

entries.title: GITLAB
entries.body: Source code management and hosting platform that facilitates collaboration between developers. GitLab is the main alternative to GitHub. The platform is quite similar, but it also offers the possibility of being self-hosted. As its name indicates, GitLab is built on the Git version control system. This platform therefore makes it possible to track code changes, manage versions and encourage collaboration through tools such as merge requests and issues. Some Bitcoin-related projects such as Samourai Wallet, Whirlpool or RoninDojo use GitLab.

entries.title: GLOBAL STATE
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Global State* designates the set of public properties of a contract, established during the *Genesis*. It acts as a public ledger and groups together the state elements that are accessible to everyone and that can be updated by authorized transitions in accordance with the rules defined by the contract's schema. Unlike *Owned States*, which are associated with specific entities, the *Global State* does not belong to any party in particular.

entries.title: GNU
entries.body:
Project initiated in 1983 by Richard Stallman to create a free operating system compatible with Unix. The project has developed many free software programs that can be used as an operating system or as a complement to another operating system. GNU is the foundation of the free software movement, which has been widely adopted in the Bitcoin community. Combined with the Linux kernel, it forms the GNU/Linux operating systems.

*The name “GNU” is a recursive acronym meaning “GNU's Not Unix”.*

entries.title: GOLDFINGER
entries.body:
Hypothetical scenario on the Bitcoin system where a malicious actor controls more than 50% of the total mining computing power (*hashrate*). With such dominance, the attacker can manipulate the consensus process, enabling malicious actions such as double spending, where the same bitcoins are spent a first time on a chain that is ultimately made obsolete, then a second time on the valid chain. Another purpose of a Goldfinger attack is transaction censorship. However, carrying out an attack of this type requires considerable financial, human, energy and technical resources, and makes the malicious actor liable to be discovered before the attack takes place. Although theoretically possible, a Goldfinger attack on Bitcoin is considered highly unlikely because of the decentralization of mining and the large amount of computing power currently deployed.

*This attack is also called the “51% Attack”.*

entries.title: GOSSIP
entries.body:
Gossip designates a distributed peer-to-peer (P2P) algorithm for spreading information in an epidemic manner to all agents of the network. For Bitcoin, Lightning and other distributed systems, this protocol makes it possible to exchange and synchronize the global state of the nodes in few cycles. Each node propagates a piece of information to one or more neighbors chosen randomly or not; these, in turn, propagate the information to other neighbors, and so on until a globally synchronized state is reached.

In the context of Lightning, gossip is a communication protocol between nodes for sharing information about the current state and topology of the network. The gossip protocol allows nodes to know the dynamic state of payment channels and of other nodes, in order to facilitate the routing of transactions through the network without requiring direct connections between all nodes.

entries.title: GPL
entries.body: Acronym for “*GNU General Public License*”. It is a series of free software licenses originally created by the Free Software Foundation. It guarantees users the freedom to use, modify and distribute the software. The GPL nevertheless requires that any derived or modified software also be distributed under the same license, which ensures that the original freedoms are preserved in all versions of the software. The GPL is often used for open source projects and is sometimes found on certain Bitcoin-related projects. However, the original license of Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin client was an MIT X11. This is incidentally still the case for Bitcoin Core.

entries.title: GRAFTROOT
entries.body:
Bitcoin protocol improvement proposal formulated by Gregory Maxwell in February 2018. Graftroot extends the concept of Taproot by adding a mechanism for delegating spending conditions. With Taproot, a group of participants who share an aggregated key can either spend directly with that key, or reveal an alternative script contained in a Merkle tree. Graftroot additionally allows these participants to delegate their spending capacity to arbitrary scripts by signing those scripts with their aggregated key.

The main usefulness of this protocol lies in the absence of a limit on the number of alternative spending conditions. Each delegation materializes as a simple Schnorr signature over the authorized script, with no overhead proportional to the number of delegated scripts. In Taproot, adding branches to the Merkle tree increases the size of the spending proof, whereas Graftroot maintains a constant cost.

Graftroot was never formalized in the form of a BIP and was not integrated into the Bitcoin protocol.

entries.title: GREEN ADDRESS
entries.body: Former Bitcoin wallet software acquired in July 2016 by Blockstream to create the current Green Wallet software.

entries.title: GREEN ADDRESSES
entries.body: Old Bitcoin address proposal in which the transactions issued from the address are pre-approved by a trusted third party. This concept allows parties receiving funds via this address to consider them immediately reliable, without waiting for them to be included in a block. It relies on the trust placed in the service that controls the *green address*, as it guarantees that the funds sent have not been and will not be double spent. This type of service was once used to speed up transactions (zero-conf), but it is no longer used today.

entries.title: GREEN WALLET
entries.body: Bitcoin wallet software available on PC, Android and iOS, developed by Blockstream since the acquisition of the GreenAddress software in 2016. It includes several features such as multisig protection with two-factor authentication. It is also compatible with most hardware wallets. It is simple software to get to grips with and can be used by beginners.

entries.title: GRIEFING ATTACK
entries.body:
Attack on the Lightning Network in which a malicious actor saturates one or more payment channels with HTLCs that never resolve, by refusing to reveal the payment preimage. The victims' funds end up frozen for the entire duration of the timelock, without the attacker stealing anything.

Each channel can only hold 483 pending HTLCs per direction. An attacker can therefore completely block a channel with a relatively small number of fake payments. The victim's only option is to force close the channel, which incurs high on-chain fees since each pending HTLC generates an additional transaction on the chain.

Although the attacker obtains no direct monetary gain, they can derive an indirect benefit by paralyzing competing routes to capture more routing fees, or by demanding a ransom to stop the attack. This vulnerability remains an open problem. The proposed countermeasures include the HTLC-GP protocol, which requires each participant to lock a financial penalty that victims can recover in the event of griefing, as well as upfront payment mechanisms.

entries.title: GROTH16
entries.body: SNARK-type zero-knowledge proof system, proposed by the cryptographer Jens Groth in 2016. Groth16 stands out for the minimal size of its proofs (only three elliptic curve elements, or about 200 bytes) and for a constant verification time, which makes it one of the most efficient schemes for on-chain verification. In return, Groth16 requires a trusted setup ceremony (*trusted setup*) specific to each circuit, during which secret parameters are generated and then ideally destroyed. If these parameters were reconstructed, it would be possible to create false proofs. The RISC Zero framework uses Groth16 as a final wrapping layer to compress large STARK proofs into compact SNARK proofs. This is the mechanism exploited by the Citrea rollup to publish validity proofs on the Bitcoin blockchain.

entries.title: GRPC
entries.body:
Remote procedure call framework (*Remote Procedure Call*) developed by Google. gRPC uses the Protocol Buffers format to serialize data and the HTTP/2 protocol for transport, offering performant and typed communications between a client and a server.

In the Lightning ecosystem, gRPC is the main interface used by LND to expose its functionality. Tools like LNCLI interact with the Lightning node through gRPC calls to manage channels, send payments, check balances or configure routing.

entries.title: GUI
entries.body: Acronym for "*Graphical User Interface*", or "interface graphique utilisateur" in French. It is a form of user interface that allows interaction with software through interactive visual elements (buttons, icons, images, windows...) and that favors the use of pointing devices (the mouse) rather than text commands as with the CLI.

entries.title: GUISETTINGS.INI.BAK
entries.body: File in Bitcoin Core used to store a backup of the graphical user interface (GUI) settings. This backup is created when using the `-resetguisettings` option, which resets the GUI settings to their default values. This file allows the user to retroactively inspect their old configurations in order to diagnose any problems related to the GUI settings.

entries.title: PRNG
entries.body: Acronym for “Pseudo-Random Number Generator”. PRNGs are a category of algorithms used to generate sequences of approximately random numbers, starting from an initial state called a seed. In cryptography, the PRNG is used to produce keys, initialization vectors and other elements requiring randomness. A good PRNG must have properties such as uniformity of outputs, unpredictability and resistance to predictive attacks. Unlike truly random number generators, PRNGs are deterministic and reproducible. On Bitcoin, PRNGs can be used in wallet management software or *hardware wallets* to generate the recovery phrase that is the basis of deterministic and hierarchical wallets.

entries.title: SEED
entries.body:
In the specific context of a Bitcoin hierarchical deterministic wallet, a seed is a 512-bit piece of information derived from randomness. It makes it possible to generate, in a deterministic and hierarchical manner, a set of private keys, and their corresponding public keys, for a Bitcoin wallet. The seed is often confused with the recovery phrase itself. Yet it is a different piece of information. The seed is obtained by applying the `PBKDF2` function to the mnemonic phrase and to the optional passphrase.

![Generation of the seed via PBKDF2 (mnemonic + passphrase) then derivation of the master key via HMAC-SHA512.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/g/graine/assets/image-1.png)

The seed was invented with BIP-0032, which defines the foundations of the hierarchical deterministic wallet. In this standard, the seed can be between 128 and 512 bits long (256 bits being recommended). This makes it possible to derive all the keys of a wallet from a single piece of information, unlike JBOK (*Just a Bunch Of Keys*) wallets, which require making new backups for every key generated. BIP-0039 subsequently came to propose an encoding of this seed, in order to make it easier for humans to read. This encoding takes the form of a phrase, generally called a mnemonic phrase or recovery phrase. This standard helps avoid errors when backing up the seed, notably thanks to the use of a checksum.

Outside the context of Bitcoin, in the field of cryptography in general, a seed is an initial value used to generate cryptographic keys, or more broadly, any type of data produced by a pseudo-random number generator. This initial value must be random and unpredictable to guarantee the security of the cryptographic system. Indeed, the seed introduces entropy into the system, but the generation process that follows is deterministic.

*In everyday language, the majority of bitcoiners refer to the mnemonic phrase when they talk about the “seed”, and not to the intermediate derivation state that sits between the mnemonic phrase and the master key.*
